title: Your first shell script
objective: By the end of this lesson you can turn commands you already type into a script that runs anywhere, takes arguments, and does not break the first time a filename contains a space.

blocks.text: A shell script is a file containing the commands you would have typed. That is the whole idea. The value is not in learning a new language — it is that a sequence you ran correctly once can now be run correctly every time, by anyone, including a scheduler at 3am.

items: The first line is the shebang: it tells the kernel which interpreter to run this with
chmod u+x backup.sh makes it executable — you met this in the permissions lesson
./backup.sh runs it. The ./ matters: it says 'in this directory', because the current directory is deliberately not searched for commands

blocks.title: Why ./ is required
blocks.text: The shell looks for commands in the directories listed in PATH, and the current directory is not one of them. That is a security decision: if it were, dropping a file named ls into a shared directory would hijack the next person who ran ls there.
Variables, and the quotes that keep them safe

blocks.caption: Assign without spaces, use with $
lines: today=$(date +%F)        # capture the output of a command
count=$(ls | wc -l)      # $( ) runs it and gives you the text back

blocks.title: The single most common shell bug
blocks.text: Write "$file", not $file. Without quotes, a value containing a space becomes two separate arguments — so rm $file on a file called holiday photos.txt tries to delete two files that do not exist, and cp $src $dst silently copies the wrong thing. Quote every variable unless you have a specific reason not to.

blocks.caption: greet.sh
lines: # $1 is the first argument, $2 the second, $@ is all of them, $# is how many

blocks.text: A script that hardcodes a path is a script that works once. A script that takes the path as $1 is a tool. That difference is most of what separates a note-to-self from something a team can use.
Reading input and reporting a result

blocks.caption: Interactive and exit codes
lines: exit 1     # failure — anything non-zero means failure

blocks.title: Exit codes are how scripts talk to each other
blocks.text: Every command sets an exit code: 0 for success, non-zero for failure. Check the last one with echo $?. This is what lets you write a && b — run b only if a succeeded — and it is how a scheduler knows your script failed rather than assuming silence means it worked.

blocks.title: Write and run one
steps: Create sysinfo.sh with an editor (nano sysinfo.sh) containing:
blocks.expected: A one-line system summary produced by your own script, and an exit code of 0. You have just written a tool that answers a question you would otherwise type out every time.

cheatsheet: #!/bin/bash on line one tells the system what runs this file
./ is required because the current directory is not in PATH — deliberately
name="value" with no spaces around the equals sign
$(command) captures a command's output into a value
$1 $2 are arguments · $@ is all of them · $# is how many
exit 0 means success · any non-zero exit code means failure
echo $? shows the exit code of the last command

checkpoint.prompt: What does the line #!/bin/bash at the top of a script do?

choices.B: It names the interpreter that runs it
choices.C: It is only a comment and has no effect here

checkpoint.explanation: The shebang names the interpreter. Making the file executable is a separate step with chmod.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is rm $file dangerous compared to rm "$file" ?

choices.A: There is no difference in bash
choices.B: Quotes make the command run faster
choices.C: Unquoted variables are always completely empty
choices.D: Values with spaces split into many arguments

checkpoint.explanation: The command acts on the wrong things. Word splitting happens before the command runs. A file named holiday photos.txt becomes two arguments, and the command does something you did not intend. checkpoint.prompt: A script finishes and echo $? prints 1. What does that mean?

choices.A: It failed — non-zero exit codes mean failure
choices.B: It succeeded and produced one line of output
choices.C: It was interrupted by the user

checkpoint.explanation: 0 is success by convention; anything else is a failure code. Schedulers and CI systems rely on this to know whether to alert.

checkpoint.prompt: Why must you type ./script.sh rather than just script.sh ?

choices.A: The current directory is kept out of PATH
choices.B: Because scripts must always have a path
choices.C: Because bash requires two characters before a filename
choices.D: Because the file is not executable otherwise

checkpoint.explanation: A dropped file cannot hijack a common command name. Leaving the current directory out of PATH prevents someone placing a malicious file named after a common command in a directory you happen to be in.
